video_metadata.working_title: MINNESOTA 1993 Cold Case Solved After 25 Years — Justice for Jeanie Childs
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: In June 1993, 35-year-old Jeanne Ann 'Jeanie' Childs was found stabbed to death in her south Minneapolis high-rise apartment, the killer leaving bloody bare footprints and DNA; 25 years later, forensic genetic genealogy and a napkin thrown away at a hockey game led to Isanti businessman Jerry Arnold Westrom, convicted of first-degree premeditated murder in August 2022.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief for a woman the world had already written off, then quiet vindication that time and science refused to forget her

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Jeanne Ann 'Jeanie' Childs (victim and heart of the story). Convicted killer: Jerry Arnold Westrom.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Jeanie Childs: 35 in June 1993 [1][13][14]. Jerry Westrom: 52 at his arrest in February 2019 [2][3]; reported as 55 or 56 at the August 2022 verdict (sources differ) [14][7]; by arithmetic he was in his mid-to-late twenties (about 26-27) in June 1993 (derived, not directly reported).
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Childs: had been involved in sex work; described by family as kind-hearted and loving [27][29]. Westrom: businessman from Isanti, Minnesota, 'hockey dad', father of three, described as well respected in his small rural community [2][27][32][48hours-X post in notes].
protagonist.location: Childs: upper-floor apartment in the Horn Towers (Charles Horn Towers) high-rise on Pillsbury Avenue South, south Minneapolis [1][13][30]. Westrom (2019): Isanti, Minnesota; arrested in Waite Park, Minnesota [2][3].
protagonist.physical_description: Not documented in sources reviewed; do not describe.
protagonist.background_brief: Childs began running away from home at around 13, according to her sister Cindy Blumer, and later became involved in sex work [27][29]. Retired Minneapolis police sergeant Robert Krebs testified he had encountered her years earlier, including a 1979 incident at a Lake Street 'health club' known for prostitution where she was cited rather than arrested [13]. Her mother is Betty Eakman; her sister Cindy Blumer; her niece Melissa Beaulieu [17][19][27].
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not documented beyond family descriptions (kind-hearted, loving, life 'complicated'). Do not speculate.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: Her mother remembered her as the daughter who was 'supposed to be there for me when I get old' [19]. Sergeant Krebs identified her through an ID in her fanny pack [13].
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: Jeanie (also spelled Jeanne / Jeannie in some reports).

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Jeanne Ann 'Jeanie' Childs
individuals.role_or_profession: Victim, 35; had been involved in sex work
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Westrom denied knowing her; DNA and bloody footprints placed him in her apartment [3][12][14]
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Stabbed to death (about 65 stab wounds) in her apartment; found June 13, 1993 [13][14][27]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Family describes her as kind-hearted and loving; ran away from home around 13 [27][29]

individuals.name: Betty Eakman
individuals.role_or_profession: Jeanie's mother; worked in hospice care in 1993
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Learned of the killing from a TV news report while caring for a hospice patient; waited 29 years for a verdict [29][19]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Gave a victim impact statement at sentencing on September 9, 2022 [17][19]
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'I was doing hospice at the time and the lady decided she wanted a television on, and they said there had been a body taken out of the building that was murdered.' [29]; 'I miss her, she's supposed to be there for me when I get old and she won't be.' [19]; 'honey, justice has been served and I'm happy about that.' [19]; 'I've waited so many years to have this end and it's put my life through so much hell and I just really feel I'll never forget and love her the way I always did.' [17][21]; 'I know that my daughter was crying for me — I know she was.' [30]

individuals.name: Cindy Blumer
individuals.role_or_profession: Jeanie's sister (also reported as Cindy Kosnitch in one report)
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Lifelong grief; publicly insisted her sister's life was complicated but she did not deserve to be killed [27][29]
individuals.humanizing_detail: At sentencing said her heart was broken for Westrom's wife and children; 'a tragedy for everyone involved', 'no winners' (paraphrased in reports) [18][20]

individuals.name: Melissa Beaulieu
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'The effect something like this creates can be vicious. They affect you for an entire lifetime. To lose someone you love is a profound experience.' [17][21]

individuals.name: Westrom's wife and three children (unnamed)
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Collateral victims acknowledged by Jeanie's sister at sentencing
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Not documented in detail; do not speculate
individuals.humanizing_detail: Blumer said her heart was broken for them [18][20]

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Women in sex work whose deaths drew little public attention
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: CBS reported the case 'garnered little, if any, press coverage at the time' [1].

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Chris Boeckers
characters.role_in_story: FBI special agent (later retired) who worked the reopened case with a Minneapolis homicide detective [27][29]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Helped review the case from 2015; said the genealogy approach was inspired by the Golden State Killer case; said the search pointed to two brothers in Minnesota [27][29]
characters.notable_quotes: Said investigators had 'no way to track down who that may or may not have been' about an unidentified man a witness described (as reported) [27]

characters.name: Robert Krebs
characters.role_in_story: Minneapolis police sergeant at the 1993 scene; retired; testified at trial [13]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Recognized the victim after finding an ID in a fanny pack; had encountered her in 1979 [13]

characters.name: Security guard (named Corey Busker in one trial-coverage summary; single-sourced)
characters.role_in_story: Entered the unit after water was reported; testified the shower was running and the bedroom window was wide open with the screen missing; said he did not leave the unit unattended [12][36]

characters.name: Mark Ulrick
characters.role_in_story: Minneapolis police supervisor of forensic science; footprint examiner [27][28]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Took Westrom's footprints and concluded friction ridge detail in the bloody prints matched Westrom's feet; four of seven prints suitable for comparison [12][27]
characters.notable_quotes: Said he is confident Westrom's footprint matches the bloody footprints (paraphrase) [27]

characters.name: Bart Epstein
characters.role_in_story: Retired forensic scientist interviewed by 48 Hours [28]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Explained that bloody bare footprints are evidence investigators rarely encounter; prints were dusted with black powder and photographed [28]

characters.name: McCarthy (defense-hired footprint expert; first name not verified)
characters.role_in_story: Hired by the defense; concluded print 'E2' belonged to Westrom, was released by the defense and later testified for the prosecution (as reported) [12][14]

characters.name: Mike Freeman
characters.key_actions_they_took: Charged Westrom; defended the napkin collection; compared the method to the Golden State Killer case [8]
characters.notable_quotes: 'When you discard things in the trash, the Supreme Court often says it's free game.' [8]; 'Today's guilty verdicts show that we will pursue convictions for serious crimes, even if it takes years to gather the evidence.' [7]

characters.name: Steve Meshbesher
characters.key_actions_they_took: Argued Arthur Gray was the killer; questioned untested knife and absence of a weapon; said they would appeal [12][35]
characters.notable_quotes: 'They just have the wrong person.' [11]; 'As we said in the beginning, and we are saying now you got the wrong guy.' [15]

characters.name: Judge Juan Hoyos
characters.role_in_story: Hennepin County District Judge at sentencing [17][19]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Sentenced Westrom on September 9, 2022 to life with parole eligibility after 30 years under 1993 law [17][18][20]
characters.notable_quotes: 'It seems like you have led a very positive life for the last 29 years.' [19]

characters.name: Judge Martha Holton Dimick
characters.role_in_story: Hennepin County judge at first appearance, February 2019 [4]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Set bail at $500,000 with conditions (prosecutors had sought / he had been held on $1 million) [4]

characters.name: Derek Fradenburg
characters.key_actions_they_took: Told WCCO the verdict came down to Westrom's police interview, the DNA and the bloody footprint [30]
characters.notable_quotes: Paraphrase only: DNA could be explained by prior contact, but the bloody bare footprints established presence during the murder [27][30]

characters.name: Arthur Gray
characters.role_in_story: Childs' boyfriend, whom she reportedly said she worked for; early person of interest; history of violence between them reported [27][28]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Told authorities he was in Milwaukee; his footprints were ruled out; BCA testified his DNA was excluded from the unknown samples [12][28]
characters.notable_quotes: None. Never charged. Defense named him as alternative perpetrator; Minnesota Supreme Court held exclusion of that evidence harmless [24].

characters.name: Unnamed man whose blood matched a stairwell sample
characters.role_in_story: Interviewed in 2015; his footprints were compared to the bedroom prints (named in CBS coverage; never charged) [27]

characters.name: Jennifer Mayerle
characters.role_in_story: WCCO investigative reporter; produced 'Footprint to Murder' documentary (released late April 2025) [30][31]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Documented the case, interviews, interrogation footage

characters.name: Erin Moriarty
characters.role_in_story: CBS 48 Hours correspondent, 'The Footprint' (first aired May 17, 2025) [32]

chronological_timeline._instructions: List every significant event with exact dates when possible. This is the backbone of your script.

events.what_happened: Jeanie Childs begins running away from home, according to her sister
events.significance: Start of a hard life; family insists it never diminished her worth

events.what_happened: Minneapolis officer Robert Krebs encounters Childs at a Lake Street 'health club' known for prostitution; she is cited rather than arrested
events.significance: Why the sergeant later recognized her

events.date: June 1993 (exact date and time of death not established in sources reviewed)
events.location: Horn Towers, Pillsbury Avenue South, south Minneapolis
events.what_happened: Childs, 35, is stabbed to death in her upper-floor apartment
events.source: [1] CBS Minnesota; [13] Star Tribune; [27] CBS News

events.what_happened: A tenant sees water flowing from Childs' unit; a security guard enters; the shower is running, the bedroom window wide open with the screen missing; Childs is found on the bedroom floor, naked except for socks, stabbed about 65 times. Bloody bare footprints are found under the bedroom window
events.significance: Discovery; the barefoot prints must belong to the killer because she wore socks
events.source: [12] Star Tribune; [13] Star Tribune; [27][28] CBS News; [24] Minn. Sup. Ct. (bedroom floor). Early reports said 'in the shower' [34] - discrepancy

events.what_happened: Evidence collected: footprints dusted with black powder and photographed; comforter; bathroom towel; washcloth; T-shirt; sink stains; a blood sample in the stairwell; a knife in the kitchen sink was photographed but never forensically tested; no murder weapon found
events.significance: The evidence that would matter decades later

events.what_happened: Investigators look at boyfriend Arthur Gray (says he was in Milwaukee; footprints ruled out) and an unidentified man described by a witness; police call the case 'horribly difficult'; little press coverage
Betty Eakman learns of the murder from a TV report while working in hospice

Minneapolis Police Department reviews unsolved cases with the FBI and the Minnesota BCA (Cold Case Task Force); Childs' case is among them; Minneapolis homicide detective and FBI special agent Chris Boeckers take a new look because of DNA advances; man whose blood matched the stairwell sample is interviewed and his footprints compared

Investigators announce an arrest in the Golden State Killer case after using genetic genealogy (general, widely reported public fact; full research reserved for the next video). Childs investigators and Hennepin County Attorney Mike Freeman explicitly cited this case as the model for their approach
events.significance: The landmark case that proved the method
events.source: General public record (to be fully sourced in next video's brief); connection to the Childs case per [27] CBS 48 Hours and [8] WFTV

events.what_happened: Police work with the FBI; a crime-scene DNA sample is sent to DNA Solutions, Inc. to build a SNP profile for comparison with commercial genealogy databases; genealogical research narrows to two possible suspects, brothers in Minnesota, one of them Jerry Westrom

events.date: January 2019 (one report gives Jan. 26, a Saturday - single-sourced)
events.location: Hockey arena, reported to be in Wisconsin
events.what_happened: Officers surveil Westrom; he orders food (a hot dog) at the concession, wipes his mouth with a napkin, puts it in a cardboard food container and throws both away; officers recover it
BCA finds a DNA mixture on the napkin; the major male profile is consistent with crime-scene DNA

Minneapolis police arrest Westrom, 52; in interview he denies knowing Childs, visiting the apartment or having sex with any women in Minneapolis in 1993, and says he does not know why his DNA would be there
events.source: [1] CBS Minnesota; [3] Star Tribune; [4] Star Tribune

events.what_happened: Hennepin County Attorney's Office charges Westrom with second-degree murder; a post-arrest DNA sample matches semen on the comforter and DNA on the bathroom towel
events.source: [2] CBS Minnesota; [3] Star Tribune; [5] Hometown Source

events.what_happened: Held on $1 million bail; Judge Martha Holton Dimick sets bail at $500,000 with conditions; Westrom released on bail
A grand jury indicts Westrom for first-degree premeditated murder
events.significance: Top charge; NOTE: the 2020 event is the indictment, not a conviction
events.source: [9] Isanti-Chisago County Star; [10] Bring Me The News

events.what_happened: Trial dates set for March and then April before trial finally begins in August 2022
Trial begins; testimony from the security guard, Sgt. Krebs, footprint examiners, BCA scientists (Gray excluded); defense blames Gray, cites untested knife; Westrom does not testify
events.source: [11] CBS Minnesota; [12][13] Star Tribune; [36] Audacy/WCCO Radio

events.what_happened: After about two hours of deliberation, jury convicts Westrom of first-degree premeditated murder and second-degree intentional murder; he is taken into custody
events.source: [7] Fox News; [14] Law&Crime; [15] KSTP; [16] Oxygen. (Forum News Service gives Aug. 22 - discrepancy)

events.what_happened: Judge Juan Hoyos sentences Westrom to life in prison with eligibility for parole after 30 years, under 1993 law; Westrom declines to speak; mother, sister and niece give statements
events.source: [17] FOX 9; [18] KARE 11; [19] Law&Crime; [20] Hometown Source; [21] Star Tribune

events.what_happened: Oral argument in State v. Westrom (A22-1679)

Court holds genetic analysis of the discarded napkin was not a search under the U.S. or Minnesota constitutions; exclusion of alternative-perpetrator evidence harmless; affirms first-degree premeditated murder conviction; reverses the second-degree conviction and remands to vacate it
events.significance: Conviction upheld; precedent on abandoned DNA

events.what_happened: Petition for certiorari filed (No. 24-271) raising Fourth Amendment shed-DNA and Confrontation Clause questions; Minnesota waives response Sept. 30, 2024
Certiorari denied

WCCO releases documentary 'Footprint to Murder' (Jennifer Mayerle) with interrogation footage; foreperson Derek Fradenburg interviewed; Westrom has asked the Great North Innocence Project to review his conviction and says he will talk after his conviction is overturned
48 Hours airs 'The Footprint' with Erin Moriarty; rebroadcasts listed in 2026 by a fan site (unverified)

Westrom serving life sentence; first-degree premeditated murder conviction affirmed and certiorari denied; no reported exoneration or new trial found in sources reviewed; earliest parole eligibility reported as 2052 (single-sourced)

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Upper-floor apartment, Horn Towers, Pillsbury Avenue South, south Minneapolis
the_moment.what_is_happening: Water flowing out of Jeanie Childs' apartment is noticed by a tenant; inside, the shower is running and the window is open
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Under the bedroom window, bare footprints in blood; she was wearing socks, so the prints were the killer's
the_moment.ironic_twist: The killer's identity was preserved in 1993 evidence, but it took a hot dog napkin tossed in a trash can at a hockey game 25 years later to put a name to it; the man had spent those years as a respected businessman and hockey dad

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who walked barefoot through Jeanie Childs' apartment in June 1993, and how could a napkin thrown away a quarter of a century later answer that?

the_method._instructions: How was the case solved? Technical details explained for a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Forensic investigative genetic genealogy (FIGG) plus abandoned-DNA confirmation and barefoot friction-ridge comparison
step_by_step_explanation: 1993: crime-scene biological evidence (comforter, towel and other items) is preserved [3][14]
2015: MPD, FBI and BCA cold case review; DNA advances make re-examination worthwhile [1][27]
2018: a crime-scene sample is sent to DNA Solutions, Inc. to create a SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) profile [3]
The SNP profile is compared with profiles in commercial genealogy databases to find relatives of the unknown man [3][27]
A genealogist builds family trees from the matches; the research points to two brothers in Minnesota, one of them Jerry Westrom [27][29]
According to the complaint as reported, either Westrom or a close relative had submitted DNA to a genealogy service [8]
January 2019: officers collect a napkin Westrom discards at a hockey game; the BCA finds a major male profile consistent with the crime-scene DNA [3][1]
After the arrest, a direct DNA sample matches semen on the comforter and DNA on the bathroom towel [5][27]
Westrom's footprints are taken; examiner Mark Ulrick finds friction ridge detail in the bloody bare prints matches his feet; a defense-hired expert reaches a matching conclusion on one print [12][27]
the_method.why_it_worked: Preserved evidence + a relative's DNA in a genealogy database + public records family-tree work + a legally collected abandoned sample + an independent physical clue (the footprints) that DNA alone could not explain away

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: Instead of the 20-odd markers police labs compare, a SNP test reads hundreds of thousands of tiny letters in the genetic code, enough to find distant cousins, like comparing an entire family photo album instead of a single photo
Using DNA matches with cousins plus birth, marriage and obituary records to rebuild a family tree until only a few people fit
DNA on something a person throws away in public; Minnesota's Supreme Court ruled that analyzing such a napkin to compare it to crime-scene DNA was not a search [24]
The soles of the feet carry ridges like fingertips; a clear bloody barefoot print can be compared like a fingerprint

technical_terms_to_explain.term: Major male profile in a mixture
technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: The napkin held DNA from more than one person, but one man's DNA dominated, and that dominant profile was consistent with the crime-scene DNA

the_method.scale_of_operation: Not quantified in sources (hours of genealogy work not reported).

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Not a single institution; the limits of 1993 forensic science and the low public attention given to the killing of a woman in sex work
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: No suspect DNA match was possible with 1993 tools; leads (boyfriend, unidentified man) went nowhere; little press coverage kept pressure low [1][27]
specific_incompetence_examples: A knife photographed in the kitchen sink was never forensically tested (defense argument, reported at trial) [35]
No murder weapon was ever found [35]
Case garnered 'little, if any, press coverage at the time' [1]
22 years passed before a structured review in 2015 [1][27]
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The evidence that solved it had sat in storage since 1993; the answer arrived from a man's own family tree and a napkin at a hockey game.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Minneapolis Police Department with the FBI and the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA); prosecution by the Hennepin County Attorney's Office
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Focus on the boyfriend Arthur Gray, later excluded by footprints and DNA [12][28]
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: SNP genealogy pointing to two Minnesota brothers, then the napkin [3][27]
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Leaving DNA and bloody bare footprints at the scene in 1993; throwing a used napkin in a public trash can in 2019
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: About 25 years and 8 months (June 1993 to February 11, 2019)

the_confrontation.scene_description: Minneapolis police arrested Westrom; details of the scene not reported
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: Denied involvement; said he did not know Childs, had not been to her apartment, had not had sex with any women in Minneapolis in 1993 and did not know why his DNA would be there [1][3]
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: A respected businessman and hockey dad in a small community; out on $500,000 bail until the verdict [4][27]

legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Security guard: shower running, window open, screen missing [12]; Sgt. Robert Krebs recognized her via ID in a fanny pack [13]; Mark Ulrick: four of seven prints suitable, matched Westrom [12][27]; defense-hired expert also matched one print and testified for the state [12]; BCA: Arthur Gray excluded as DNA contributor [12]; prosecutor: 'You step in liquid blood and you put your foot down. His footprints were in her blood because he killed her.' [12]

victim_impact_statements.key_quote: I miss her, she's supposed to be there for me when I get old and she won't be.
honey, justice has been served and I'm happy about that.
The effect something like this creates can be vicious. They affect you for an entire lifetime. To lose someone you love is a profound experience.
(paraphrase) Her heart is broken for Westrom's wife and children; a tragedy for everyone involved; there are no winners

legal_resolution.sentence_received: Life in prison with parole eligibility after 30 years, under the law in effect in 1993 (current law would require life without parole) [17][18][20]. One Forum News Service article says 'without the possibility of parole' - contradicted by FOX 9, KARE 11 and Hometown Source.
legal_resolution.protagonist_statement_in_court: Westrom declined to address the court [17][19]
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: serving a life sentence for first-degree premeditated murder; Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed that conviction on May 8, 2024 (second-degree conviction vacated as legally duplicative); U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari October 21, 2024; Westrom maintains innocence and asked the Great North Innocence Project to review his case (no exoneration or new-trial order found in sources reviewed); earliest parole eligibility reported as 2052 (single source).

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: A woman many treated as a headline category was a daughter, sister and aunt; her case shows that who the victim was should never decide how hard we look
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Any DNA you or a relative upload to a genealogy site can help identify a relative; anything you throw away in public may be tested (Minnesota Supreme Court, 2024)
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Preserve evidence; never let the victim's circumstances shrink the investigation
universal_stakes.current_relevance: State v. Westrom (2024) is a leading state ruling on abandoned DNA; the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review it in October 2024; Westrom continues to claim innocence
